description: Hello! We are team n//a, a group of students with a huge passion for space exploration, creative problem-solving, and turning big ideas into real projects. We bring skills in research, along with experience working on school STEM projects and participating in many science competitions.
summary: LAIKA: Mission Red Planet is a free, browser-based 8-bit strategy game that teaches insights into how to survive on Mars. Players run a small Mars outpost for 10 sols (Martian days). They balance solar power, battery storage, life support, food, and radiation protection, while dust storms, equipment failures, and solar particle events force real trade-offs. Every mechanic is based on NASA findings: Opportunity's 2018 dust storm, Curiosity's radiation measurements, water recycling on the International Space Station, the Veggie plant system, and NASA's Mars surface power study. An in-game science lab clearly explains what NASA actually observed from what the game simplifies. The story is a clearly labeled alternate history starring Laika, the real dog who flew on Sputnik 2 in 1957 and did not survive. In our story, she reaches Mars and comes home, and the game closes with a memorial to her. LAIKA turns abstract space engineering into decisions a user can feel. Every upgrade, shortage, and emergency shows why sustainable, reliable systems matter for future human exploration. It needs no account, download, or personal data, so any classroom can use it.
details:
MAIN MENU

LAIKA: Mission Red Planet is a pixel-art Mars base-building game made for the “Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer” challenge. You are the mission commander of a fictional outpost. Your job is to keep Laika safe for 10 sols and bring her back to planet Earth.

How it works

Each sol, the player:

  • Inspects six buildings: Habitat, Solar Array, Battery Station, Life Support, Radiation Shelter, and Greenhouse.
  • Builds once: Upgrade or repair one building. An upgrade makes it better; a repair fixes damage. This is a deliberate lesson in engineering trade-offs.
  • Manages power use: Switches the greenhouse between OFF, LOW, and HIGH, trading power for food.
  • Answers emergencies Such as a dust storm, a broken water recycler, an air leak, or a solar particle warning. Each has three choices with clear costs and consequences.
  • Previews, then advances: Checks what the next sol will do, then advances and reads a simple before-and-after report.

THE OUTPOST

Five resources are tracked: Power, Life Support, Food, Radiation Hazard, and Materials. Dust lowers solar output (clear sky x1.0, dusty x0.75, dust storm x0.40). Batteries store energy for bad days. Damaged equipment works less well. If life support, power, or food runs out, or radiation gets too high, Mission Control safely brings Laika back to an orbiting ship. Users learn that failure has causes they can fix.

AN EMERGENCY MISSION

A built-in science lab links every system to a real, cited NASA source:

Each card shows three things side by side: what NASA observed, how the game simplifies it, and which game mechanic it explains. All in-game numbers are labelled as fictional game units, so we never present gameplay as real measurements.

SCIENCE LAB CARD

Feedback that teaches

  • Upgrades: Players can see the actual benefit of the building the user upgrades. For example, Life Support goes from recycling 5 to 8 per sol, and Laika runs over to celebrate.
  • Hints: A hint button reads the real game state and spotlights one useful control, such as low power pointing to the solar array. It never plays for the user.
  • Mission report: At the end, a 100-point report breaks down life support, power, radiation, food, materials, and emergency response. It names the player's best decision and one thing to improve.

MISSION REPORT

Story and emotion

  • Introduction: A 20-second opening shows Laika's 1957 capsule, then a journey to Mars.
  • Success ending: An astronaut rescues Laika, and the grade is revealed on the flight home. She returns to Earth to a cheering crowd and finally gets a loving family.
  • The memorial: The ending closes on a real photograph of Laika and the words "In Loving Memory of Laika."
  • Failure: A gentle scene shows Laika sad but safe, then encourages another try.

The fiction is labelled as alternate history throughout.

SUCCESS ENDING STORYBOARD

Benefits and intended impact

  • Easy to reach: It is free and runs in any browser on ordinary school laptops, tablets, and phones. No account, download, tracking, or personal data; progress is saved only in the browser.
  • Reaches readers’ text preferences: Easy, normal, and hard difficulties; simple or detailed explanations; three text sizes; reduced-motion support; and keyboard and touch controls.
  • Teaches the core idea: Players see how power, life support, food, and radiation protection depend on each other, the same system thinking real mission planners use.

We want players to finish a mission thinking, "I could be an amazing critical and logical-thinking engineer," and to know the real science behind it.

ACCESSIBILITY

Tools and technologies

  • Code: TypeScript, Next.js 15, React 19, and Tailwind CSS. Hosted on Vercel.
  • Art and sound: All pixel art is original and drawn in code as SVG. We synthesize sound effects live with the Web Audio API, and our team made the music.
  • Testing: 121 automated tests check the game engine, upgrades, saves, and scoring. We used browser testing at five screen sizes and balance simulations of 8 strategies x 300 games on each difficulty.
  • AI: Claude (Anthropic), used through Claude Code, assisted with code and testing under our direction.

What makes it creative?

  • It turns a sad real story into a respectful, hopeful one and still tells users the truth about Laika.
  • Every game rule maps to a real NASA finding, which the Science Lab explains.
  • It teaches trade-offs through choices and consequences rather than long explanations.

Factors we considered

  • Age-appropriate: short text, visual hints, and kind consequences.
  • Sensitive history: a clear fiction label and a memorial for the real Laika.
  • Scientific honesty: sources are cited, and real data is kept separate from game rules.
  • Accessibility and privacy: text size, reduced motion, and keyboard play, with no personal data collected.
  • Fairness: difficulty is tuned with simulations so beginners can win and experts are challenged.

Play it here: https://laika-mars.vercel.app/
